- Problem: Shortest Job First (non-preemptive). Processes: P1(AT=0, BT=8), P2(AT=1, BT=7), P3(AT=8, BT=5), P4(AT=12, BT=8), P5(AT=13, BT=8), P6(AT=13, BT=1).

If two processes have the same next burst, FCFS breaks the tie. SJF can be non-preemptive (SJN) or preemptive (SRTF). A better name is shortest-next-CPU-burst. SJF is optimal (minimum average waiting time) but the real difficulty is knowing the length of the next CPU request, so it cannot be implemented exactly at the short-term level; it is approximated by predicting the next burst from previous ones. Example 5 (all at 0): P1 10, P2 5, P3 8: Gantt P2 0–5, P1 5–13, P3 13–23; average TAT 13.67, average WT 6. Example 6 (different arrivals): P1 (0, 10), P2 (1, 3), P3 (2, 6), P4 (3, 4), P5 (4, 2). Gantt P1 0–10, P5 10–12, P2 12–15, P4 15–19, P3 19–25. TAT 10, 14, 23, 16, 8 (average 14.2); WT 0, 11, 17,
[2] (Notes: Seed course notes · SJF) Shortest Job First (SJF, non-preemptive) — Rule: Whenever the CPU becomes free, SJF picks the process with the shortest burst time among the processes that have already ARRIVED. A process that has not arrived yet cannot be chosen, even if its burst is shorter. Once a process starts, it runs to completion. Ties are broken by arrival order (FCFS).

FACTS (verified by the OS Engine; use only these numbers):

COURSE NOTES:
[1] (Teacher's notes: Class notes, BCSE303L Module 3 – CPU scheduling (Fall 2026-27) · Priority scheduling) Module 3 class notes: CPU scheduling — Comparison of preemptive algorithms (slide 22): SRTF: always runs the process with the shortest remaining burst; a newly arrived process with a shorter remaining time preempts immediately; minimum average waiting and turnaround time; frequent context switches; long processes may starve. Preemptive priority: runs the highest-priority process; a newly arrived higher-priority process preempts immediately; low-priority processes may starve. Round Robin: each process gets a fixed time quantum, then is preempted and moved to the end of the ready queue; no starvation; fair sharing; performance depends on the quantum; many context switches; a new process joins the ready queue and waits its turn. MLFQ: several queues with different priorities and quanta; the highest-priority queue is served first; processes move between queues based on CPU usage; very low starvation (aging and promotion); hard to implement and tune; used in modern general-purpose OSs.
[2] (Teacher's notes: Class notes, BCSE303L Module 3 – CPU scheduling (Fall 2026-27) · Priority scheduling) Module 3 class notes: CPU scheduling — Priority scheduling (slides 57–58): A priority is associated with each process and the CPU goes to the highest-priority process; equal priorities are served FCFS. SJF is a priority algorithm where priority is the inverse of the predicted next CPU burst. Priority scheduling can be preemptive (a newly arrived process with higher priority than the running one preempts it) or non-preemptive (the new process is simply put at the head of the ready queue). The notes show both conventions, smallest integer = highest priority and largest integer = highest priority; the worked examples use smallest integer = highest priority unless the question says otherwise. Problem: starvation of low-priority processes. Solution: aging, increasing the priority of a process as time passes.

A time quantum (time slice), generally 10–100 ms, is the maximum CPU time a process gets in one turn before it is preempted. A time quantum (time slice), generally 10–100 ms, is the maximum CPU time a process gets in one turn before it is preempted. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: new processes are added to the tail; the scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it.
